div.head: SUBSECT. 3.
Symptoms of Melancholy abounding in the whole body.
div.p:
Their bodies that are affected with this universal melancholy, are most part black, Wecker.the melancholy juice is redundant all over, hirsute they are, and lean, they have broad veins, their blood is gross and thick. Montaltus, cap. 22.Their spleen is weak, and a Liver apt to engender the humour; they have kept bad diet, or have had some evacuation stopped, as haemorrhoids, or months in women, which Lib. 1 cap. 16. Interrogare convenit, an aliqua evacuationis retentio obvenerit, viri in haemorroides mulierum menstruis, & vide faciem similiter an sit rubicunda [It is appropriate to enquire whether any retention of an evacuation has occurred, in men in the haemorrhoids, in women in the menses; and look similarly at whether the face is ruddy].Trallianus in the cure, would have carefully to be enquired, and withal to observe of what complexion the part is, of black or red. For as Forestus and Hollerius contend, if they be black, it proceeds from abundance of natural melancholy; if it proceed from cares, agony, discontents, diet, exercise, &c., they may be as well of any other colour: red, yellow, pale, as black, and yet their whole blood corrupt: praerubi colore saepe sunt tales, saepe flavi [such people are often extremely red in colour, {others} often yellow] (saith Montaltus cap. 22. Piso. Ex colore sanguinis si minuas venas, si fluat niger, &c. [From the colour of the blood if you open a vein, if it runs black, etc.]Montaltus cap. 22). The best way to discern this species, is to let them bleed, if the blood be corrupt, thick and black, and they withal free from those hypochondriacal symptoms, & not so grievously troubled with them, or those of the head, it argues they are melancholy a toto corpore [in the whole body]. The fumes which arise from this corrupt blood, disturb the mind, and make them fearful and sorrowful, heavy-hearted, as the rest, dejected, discontented, solitary, silent, weary of their lives, dull & heavy, or merry, &c., and if far gone, that which Apuleius wished to his enemy, by way
of imprecation, is true in them; Apul. lib. 1.Dead men’s bones, hobgoblins, ghosts are ever in their minds, & meet them still in every turn: all the bugbears of the night, and terrors, fairybabes of tombs, and graves are before their eyes, and in their thoughts, as to women and children, if they be in the dark alone. If they hear, or read, or see any tragical object, it sticks by them, they are afraid of death, and yet weary of their lives, in their discontented humours they quarrel with all the world, bitterly inveigh, tax satirically, and because they cannot otherwise vent their passions, or redress what is amiss, as they mean, they will by violent death at last be revenged on themselves.
